name: The Tiebout Model
statement: Residents sort themselves among competing local governments by moving to the community whose bundle of public goods and taxes best matches their preferences.
statementAccent: moving to the community whose bundle of public goods and taxes best matches their preferences
meaning: The Tiebout model proposes a market-like, non-political solution to the free-rider problem in providing local public goods: because people can choose where to live, they effectively "shop" among municipalities offering different tax and service packages. Rational relocation causes people to sort into communities of like-minded residents, revealing their true preferences for public goods much as market purchases reveal preferences for private goods.
mechanism: Tiebout modeled consumer-voters as choosing among many local jurisdictions, each offering a fixed bundle of public services at a given tax rate, assuming costless mobility, full information, no spillovers between jurisdictions, and enough jurisdictions to match diverse preferences. Under these conditions, households migrate toward the jurisdiction that maximizes their utility, and this competitive sorting drives municipalities toward efficient, optimally sized provision of local public goods.

examples.text: Charles Tiebout introduced the model in "A Pure Theory of Local Expenditures," Journal of Political Economy, vol. 64, no. 5 (1956), pp. 416–424.

The model is most often invoked to explain U.S. metropolitan areas with many independent suburban municipalities, where households sort by school quality, tax rates, and service levels when choosing where to live.

The framework has been used to explain patterns such as wealthier residents concentrating in communities offering higher-amenity public services, while lower-income residents locate elsewhere given differing tax/service trade-offs.

whyItMatters: The Tiebout model is a foundational result in public economics and fiscal federalism, providing the theoretical basis for arguments in favor of decentralized local government, tax competition among municipalities, and property-tax-funded local public goods.
limits: Its assumptions — costless and unrestricted mobility, perfect information, no inter-jurisdictional spillovers, and enough communities to satisfy every preference — are unrealistic; moving is costly, information is imperfect, and services like pollution control routinely spill across municipal boundaries. It also applies poorly to rural or consolidated urban areas without many competing jurisdictions.
misreadings: It is sometimes misapplied as literal proof that any observed residential sorting is efficient or preference-driven, when in practice zoning, discrimination, and moving costs can produce sorting for reasons unrelated to genuine preference-matching.
origin: Charles M. Tiebout, 1956 ("A Pure Theory of Local Expenditures").
